ai-at-work.title: The AI layoff wave is becoming a powder keg
ai-at-work.excerpt: What makes this combustible: at the very moment that tens of thousands of workers are being shown the door, a small cohort of AI insiders is becoming wealthy on a scale that's hard to comprehend.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Tech companies are laying off thousands of workers while a tiny group of AI insiders are getting absurdly rich, creating a massive wealth and opportunity gap. For those of us managing digital workplaces, this matters because your employees are watching this play out and asking hard questions about job security, fairness, and whether their employer actually values them or just sees them as replaceable. The irony is thick enough to cut with a knife: companies are claiming they need AI to do more with less, but what they're really doing is concentrating both power and money upward while the rest of the workforce holds its breath.

ai-at-work.title: White House forces Anthropic to disable new frontier models following abrupt export ban
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic PBC was forced just to abruptly pull the plug on foreign access to two of its most powerful artificial intelligence models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, just days after it launched them. The sudden
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The U.S. Commerce Department abruptly blocked Anthropic from offering its latest AI models internationally, forcing the company to pull Fable 5 and Mythos 6 from foreign access almost immediately after launch. This matters because it signals that AI capability controls are now a serious policy lever, which means digital workplace teams need to start planning for a fragmented global AI tooling landscape instead of the seamless international access they've gotten used to. Welcome to the era where your fancy new AI assistant works great in the US office but your London team gets the older version, which is exactly the kind of operational headache that keeps CIOs up at night.

ai-at-work.title: 10 best practices for optimizing generative and agentic AI costs
ai-at-work.excerpt: As enterprises scale initiatives, the cost of developing, deploying and operating generative artificial intelligence models rises significantly. The shift toward AI agents can further increase costs b
ai-at-work.dwp_take: SiliconAngle ran a piece on how to keep generative AI costs from spiraling out of control as companies scale up their AI initiatives and shift toward AI agents. This matters because most organizations are burning cash on AI projects right now with zero governance, and IT leaders need actual frameworks instead of just throwing money at the latest models. Here's the thing though: if your company needs an article to tell you that "poor architecture" and "weak governance" cost money, you've already lost the plot somewhere.

tools-tech.title: Nextcloud CEO: Open source moves from ‘a nerdy audience’ to the geopolitical stage
tools-tech.excerpt: MUNICH — Amid trans-Atlantic political and trade tensions, digital sovereignty — once a relatively niche concern — has jumped to the top of the agenda for European organizations wary of their reliance
tools-tech.dwp_take: Nextcloud's CEO is saying that open source software has become a geopolitical issue in Europe as organizations worry about depending too much on American tech companies. This matters to digital workplace pros because it signals a real shift in how enterprises pick their collaboration tools, moving away from the "we'll just use what everyone uses" mentality. Here's the thing though: Europe's suddenly discovering open source right as it becomes trendy doesn't mean the integration headaches and support gaps disappear, so buckle up.

digital-culture.title: Stop waiting, feel ready: 3 lessons to unlock creativity today
digital-culture.excerpt: Some of us treat creativity like a reward. Something we’ll fully inhabit once a major milestone is reached or when the weekend comes around. Through years of working with leaders, I’ve realized that t
digital-culture.dwp_take: The article argues that people wrongly treat creativity as something to pursue later, after hitting milestones or clocking out, when they should be practicing it now as a daily habit. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because remote and hybrid teams need creative problem-solving to function, and you can't build that muscle if everyone's waiting for Friday to think differently. Here's the thing: most organizations claim they want innovation while simultaneously scheduling it into the calendar like it's a dentist appointment, which is exactly backwards.

industry-news.title: 'Botsitting' is destroying productivity as workers spend nearly a full day each week making AI 'usable'
industry-news.excerpt: While workers are reporting productivity improvements, ‘botsitting’ means these are often negated
industry-news.dwp_take: Workers are spending roughly a full workday per week babysitting AI tools to make them actually work, according to new research highlighted in ITPro. This matters because if your workforce is burning that much time correcting, prompting, and managing AI instead of doing actual work, you've got an expensive problem that nobody budgeted for. Here's the truth: companies bought shiny AI tools without thinking about the human labor tax required to make them useful, which is basically the digital workplace version of buying a fancy car that only runs if someone pushes it.

industry-news.title: The AI pricing time bomb
industry-news.excerpt: How should enterprises approach AI agents, and in particular, their AI budgets?
industry-news.dwp_take: Enterprises are waking up to the fact that AI agent deployments cost way more to run than initial pilots suggested, with pricing models that punish scale and usage. Digital workplace leaders need to understand these economics before they commit to AI tools, because a chatbot that seemed cheap at 100 users gets real expensive at 10,000 users, and finance will blame you for the surprise. The dirty secret nobody wants to admit at conference panels is that most companies will end up paying more for AI than they saved automating the thing in the first place.

industry-news.title: Nottingham University cyber attack: Everything we know so far as ShinyHunters claims responsibility
industry-news.excerpt: The personal data of past and present students has been accessed in the latest attack on the education sector
industry-news.dwp_take: Nottingham University fell victim to a cyber attack where the ShinyHunters group breached student records, exposing personal data of current and former students. This matters to digital workplace pros because universities are training grounds for tomorrow's workforce, and when their security fails, it signals what attackers will try on corporate networks next. Here's the thing though: if a major institution can't protect student data, imagine what's happening at companies spending less on security than they do on office snacks.

industry-news.title: MSPs grow wary over supply chain security threats
industry-news.excerpt: CyberSmart’s 2026 MSP Survey found that more than two-in-five firms experienced a cyber incident linked to a supplier or third-party vendor over the past year
industry-news.dwp_take: More than 40% of MSPs got hit with cyber incidents coming through their supply chain over the past year, and they're rightfully nervous about it now. This matters because your digital workplace runs on a chain of vendors and integrations, and one weak link from your MSP's suppliers can compromise everything you've built. Here's the thing: we spent decades building fortresses around our networks while leaving the back door wide open to whoever our vendors let in.
